analysis.title: What to watch in the week ahead (Weekly Global)
key_insights: UBS reads the recent tech sell-off and rebound as a positioning reset, not the end of the AI investment cycle. It warns that elevated expectations and concentrated positioning leave AI-linked stocks open to further sharp moves.

NVIDIA reports on 17 November and is the next test of the AI rebound. Investors want reassurance that compute-capacity demand continues under new leadership after CEO Jensen Huang's resignation on Thursday, plus data on data center demand, order visibility, margins, supply constraints and customer capex plans.

UBS forecasts aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026, USD 1.4tr in 2027 and USD 1.5tr in 2028. Investors are weighting monetization, balance sheet strength, financing, execution and capacity utilization more heavily as the cycle matures.

UBS favors established technology platforms with tangible AI revenues, strong balance sheets, existing computing capacity and the ability to fund investment internally. It advises keeping diversified AI exposure and using strength to trim single-stock concentration and oversized technology allocations.

October US CPI was stronger than expected: headline +0.4% m/m, core +0.3% m/m. Three-month annualized core inflation rose to 3.75% from below 2% in August, raising the risk of consecutive 25bp Fed hikes instead of quarterly moves.

Dallas Fed President Logan said the pace of tightening might need to accelerate, and Governor Waller raised the possibility of a 50bp hike in December. This week's Fed minutes and speeches will show whether support for faster tightening is broadening.

UBS still expects 25bp Fed hikes in December and March, though the risk of consecutive moves has grown. It sees limited support for a 50bp move and does not expect an extended hiking cycle, since higher yields and tighter financing are already restraining activity.

UBS favors quality short- and medium-maturity bonds for income and protection against further yield increases. It is cautious on the longest maturities because of wide fiscal deficits and heavy government bond issuance.

The UK inflation report is a test of whether persistent price pressure is a broader developed-market problem. Strong readings could lift gilt yields and reinforce Bank of England tightening expectations, while softer data would suggest a shallow cycle.

The Stoxx 600 set a record high last week and the Euro Stoxx 50 has rebounded from its October dip. Support comes from strong Q3 earnings, falling oil prices, recovering margins and a share of companies beating estimates above the historical average.
UBS expects Eurozone earnings to grow 15% next year and stays positive on the region's equities. It favors banks, information technology, industrials, consumer discretionary, health care and Germany.
